notes.made: Josh Davis built Endtroducing almost entirely on an Akai MPC60 MKII, starting in his apartment and finishing at the Glue Factory, Dan the Automator's home studio in San Francisco. This one stands on the piano from David Axelrod's 'The Human Abstract' (1969), with the bass line from Pekka Pohjola's 'The Madness Subsides' and voices from Meredith Monk's 'Dolmen Music', plus pieces of Baraka, Organized Konfusion and Marlena Shaw's 'California Soul'. The records came from Rare Records in Sacramento, where he spent hours a day digging.
notes.context: It was the album's first single, out on James Lavelle's Mo' Wax on 2 September 1996, and reached 54 in the UK. B Plus directed the video, which MTV's Amp played heavily, and the US sleeve shows John Hillyard, who ran the shop where Shadow found many of the samples. Guinness later listed Endtroducing as the first album made completely from samples.

listen_for.note: The mournful piano is David Axelrod's, from 'The Human Abstract'. Everything else is arranged around it.
The bass line is lifted from Pekka Pohjola's 'The Madness Subsides', a jazz-rock record few hip-hop producers would have owned.
Those come from Meredith Monk's 'Dolmen Music', an avant-garde vocal piece, sitting on top of a hip-hop drum beat.

leads_to.title: The Human Abstract

notes.unverified: I couldn't confirm where in the track each sample enters, so the listen notes describe layers rather than sections.
